Community Care Centres (CCCs) are small facilities, with a maximum of 10 beds, located within communities and operated by community health workers. These centres provide isolation facilities for Ebola patients to prevent further transmission of the virus within households and communities. CCCs also offer basic curative and palliative care in an environment supported by the patient’s family and community. CCCs are part of a broader Community Approach, which includes four key pillars of the Ebola response strategy: 1. Case finding, including mechanisms for monitoring Ebola contacts and early detection of new cases at the community level. 2. Isolation and care of Ebola patients. 3. Safe and dignified burials, with respect for local traditions and adequate burial teams. 4. Social mobilization and community engagement to ensure acceptance and sustainability of interventions. The concept of CCCs is flexible and should be adapted to the local environment and context of each country. However, strict supervision and adherence to key principles are essential to ensure the safety of the approach. CCCs represent a novel approach in the context of the Ebola response, and evaluation is necessary. WHO and its partners recommend conducting a “lessons learned” exercise after implementing several pilot centres. Validated proof of the concept will enable the large-scale implementation of CCCs. Key considerations for implementing CCCs include: Community engagement and empowerment: Communities should be involved in all stages of the process, including planning, implementation, maintenance, and operation. Facility design: CCCs are small structures (maximum of 10 beds) where Ebola patients can be housed separately from their families and community. These facilities must have appropriate water and sanitation systems, waste management, and disinfection protocols. Triage and patient flow: A triage protocol will assess patients’ risk of having Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) before entry. Suspected and confirmed cases, as well as patients with “wet” symptoms (e.g., vomiting, bleeding, diarrhea), are separated to reduce transmission risks. Standard of care: Patients must receive respectful, compassionate care 24/7 from trained community members or health staff. At a minimum, CCCs provide food, water, oral rehydration, presumptive malaria treatment (where appropriate), antipyretics, analgesics, and broad-spectrum oral antibiotics under medical supervision. Intravenous fluids may be administered when supplies and trained staff are available. Psychosocial support is also provided for patients and their families, along with community awareness initiatives and family kits for patients and deceased individuals’ families. Staffing and safety are critical. CCC staff include caregivers, cleaners, communicators, and security personnel as needed. All staff are trained in Ebola management and infection prevention and control (IPC) and are supervised daily. A supervision team regularly visits CCCs to mentor health workers, educate the community, collect samples for laboratory confirmation, and assess safety and adherence to standards. Supplies and personal protective equipment (PPE) are provided to minimize transmission risks and ensure appropriate care. CCCs differ from other Ebola facilities, such as holding or referral centres, which isolate cases before transferring them to an Ebola Treatment Unit (ETU) once laboratory confirmation and transportation are available. CCCs address geographical and capacity challenges faced by ETUs, particularly in remote areas where ETUs are inaccessible or overwhelmed. CCCs provide isolation and care close to patients’ homes, improving community acceptance and reducing the need to transport infectious patients, which has previously led to secondary infections among transport personnel. Home-based care, while an option in some contexts, poses significant risks of Ebola transmission to household members and the community. It is unrealistic to expect households in confined environments to adequately protect themselves from infection. Without active mentoring, medical supervision, PPE supply chains, decentralized laboratory testing, waste management, and safe burial procedures, home-based care is likely to increase community transmission. Properly implemented CCCs can slow the progression of the epidemic by reducing community contact with infected individuals and providing care close to patients’ homes. This approach improves community acceptance and reduces the basic reproduction number (R0) below 1, which is critical for ending the epidemic. Modeling studies suggest that reducing the time from symptom onset to admission can significantly impact transmission rates. To ensure safety, community workers receive training in Ebola case management and IPC. Each CCC is regularly supervised by a team, ideally daily, consisting of at least one clinician and one IPC specialist. These teams ensure the safe management of the facility. IPC monitoring and assessment tools are available for use in CCCs, and water, sanitation, hygiene, and waste management are prioritized. CCCs will not open if there are doubts about the safety and security of staff and patients. Efforts are made to avoid diverting resources from other health facilities. Unemployed local healthcare workers can be recruited to staff CCCs, and supply planning is conducted in advance to ensure adequate resources for all care facilities. The CCC approach complements ETUs by addressing all transmission risks and providing a comprehensive solution embedded in the Community Approach. Family members are generally not allowed inside CCCs in some countries, such as Liberia and Sierra Leone. Alternative solutions, such as transparent walls or mobile phones for communication, can be implemented to maintain connections between patients and their families. Open communication with the community is essential, and families should be kept informed about CCC activities and the condition of their loved ones. If family members are allowed to care for patients, only one designated caregiver should be permitted to reduce household transmission risks.
